Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Cloud Concepts & Attack Vectors
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Cloud Computing Concepts & Attack Vectors

Learn what responsibilities shift across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, and where attackers commonly find openings in cloud setups.

In this lesson

Service models, Shared Responsibility, common cloud attack vectors, misconfigurations, IAM risks, and safe testing practices for ethical hackers.

Coming up

Concrete examples like open storage buckets and insecure network rules, plus a careful hands-on activity to observe misconfigurations in public data responsibly.

Explore Key Topics
Service Models
How IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS shift responsibility and where you should test.
Shared Responsibility
Who secures what, and why customer misconfigurations are the biggest risk.
Attack Vectors
IAM flaws, open buckets, insecure APIs, and missing logs — practical examples included.
Concept Map
IaaS
IaaS
You manage OS, apps, data.
PaaS
PaaS
Platform-level responsibilities shift to provider.
SaaS
SaaS
Provider delivers full application.
Shared Responsibility
Provider secures the cloud; customer secures resources in it. Most breaches stem from customer configuration and code.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives give you a clear map of what competence looks like for cloud security assessment. First, you will learn to differentiate cloud service models and deployment options so you can determine who owns each security control. A concrete example is recognizing that in IaaS you must patch the operating system, while a SaaS application’s runtime is managed by the provider. Second, you will explain the Shared Responsibility Model and apply it during testing. That means you will identify provider-controlled components versus customer-managed components before designing an engagement. Third, you will identify typical cloud attack vectors like insecure IAM, open storage buckets, and exposed APIs, and practice how to detect them. Finally, you will analyze misconfigurations and interpret logging gaps so you can score findings accurately and recommend actionable remediation. Each objective ties to a practical task: classify a resource, examine an IAM policy, check a storage ACL, and review cloud logs for suspicious activity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These practical objectives translate knowledge into testable skills. You will practice inspecting IAM policies to spot overly permissive roles and unrotated keys, and you will test for multi-factor authentication gaps. You will perform safe discovery for misconfigured storage — observing publicly exposed buckets without downloading or modifying data. You will audit network security rules to find unintended inbound access, such as wide-open SSH or database ports. You will also learn to evaluate logging coverage so you can judge whether an attacker could remain undetected. Each objective includes a verification step: read a policy, confirm MFA, query a bucket’s public ACL, and check whether activity logging is enabled. That verification step is what counts toward competency. Remember: do not make changes to a customer environment without explicit authorization; instead, reproduce findings with permissive test accounts or in a controlled lab.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Learning Objectives — Practical Skills

Objective verification

Each practice objective includes a specific verification step you can perform in a test environment.

Inspect IAM
Read policies, find wildcard principals, check for console access without MFA. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Check storage ACLs
Verify bucket policy and public access settings. Never download unknown data. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Audit network rules
Look for security groups and firewall rules allowing broad inbound access. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Confirm logging
Check for activity logs and retention settings to determine detection capabilities. VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Safety and scope

Always work in a scoped engagement or a dedicated lab. Use temporary credentials with least privilege for tests, and avoid modifying or downloading unknown customer data.

Common assessor mistake
Focusing on provider infrastructure rather than customer configurations. Most breaches result from customer-side misconfigurations and application vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
screens.narratorSegment: Start by making the service models concrete. Infrastructure as a Service gives you virtual machines and networking; you are responsible for the operating system, applications, and data on those machines. Platform as a Service provides a managed runtime and platform components — you typically deploy code but do not manage the underlying OS. Software as a Service delivers a complete application where the provider manages almost everything, but you must still control user identities and data within the app. A practical example: if a company runs a web server on an IaaS virtual machine, it must apply OS patches and configure firewalls. If the same company deploys the web app to a PaaS offering, the provider manages the runtime patching, but the app code and configuration remain the customer's responsibility. A common misconception is to assume SaaS needs no security testing; in reality, misconfigured user roles, weak authentication, or exposed integrations in SaaS can still lead to breaches. Key takeaway: determine which model a target resource implements before you design tests. That classification directly informs which controls you inspect and which findings you report.

keyIdea.title: Model determines responsibility
keyIdea.text: Classify each resource as IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS to know which security layers you must assess.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Cloud Service Models
Definition

IaaS · PaaS · SaaS

Each model shifts responsibilities. Identify who patches, who configures, and who manages data access.

IaaS (example: virtual machines)
Customer manages OS, apps, data; provider manages physical hosts and hypervisor.
PaaS (example: managed app services)
Provider manages platform runtime; customer manages app code and configuration.
SaaS (example: collaboration tools)
Provider supplies application; customer manages user accounts and data policies.
Concrete example
Web app on IaaS vs PaaS
On IaaS you patch the OS and configure the VM firewall. On PaaS the runtime patching is handled by the provider but you still secure application code and environment variables. On SaaS you control user roles and integrations.
Mistake to avoid
Assuming SaaS requires no testing. Misconfigured roles or exposed integrations inside SaaS can result in data exposure.
Key Takeaway

Classify model first. That classification tells you which layers to inspect: OS and network for IaaS, app config for PaaS, and identity and data controls for SaaS.

screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model
screens.narratorSegment: The Shared Responsibility Model is the foundation for cloud security testing. In simple terms, the cloud provider secures the underlying infrastructure — the physical data centers, hardware, and core virtualization — while the customer secures resources they deploy inside that infrastructure, such as data, applications, operating systems, and network configuration. For example, a provider ensures the hypervisor is patched and that physical access controls exist, but it is the customer’s duty to rotate their access keys, configure secure network rules, and harden application code. For an ethical hacker this distinction matters because misconfigurations and application vulnerabilities in the customer’s responsibility area are where you will find the majority of exploitable issues. A common misconception is to test provider infrastructure in a live engagement; doing so can violate terms and cause harm. Instead, identify which controls the customer manages and prioritize those for inspection. Practical step: create a simple mapping for each resource you encounter that labels which side manages the OS, network policies, data encryption, identity, and logging. That map becomes your test scope and helps avoid false positives or misattributed findings.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Shared Responsibility Model
Definition

Security of the cloud vs. security in the cloud

Provider secures infrastructure; customer secures what they deploy on it. Use this to scope tests and assign remediation responsibility.

Provider responsibilities
Physical security, host infrastructure, and hypervisor integrity.
Customer responsibilities
OS patching, application security, network rules, IAM, and data protection.
Practice
Ownership mapping exercise
For any resource, label who controls the OS, patching, network access, encryption, identity, and logging. Use that map to prioritize customer-controlled findings.
Misconception
Assuming provider handles all security. In IaaS especially, customers manage crucial layers like the OS and application stack.
Key Takeaway

Always map resource ownership first. That map prevents testing blind spots and misattributed blame for findings.

screens.title: Identity and Access Management (IAM) Risks
screens.narratorSegment: Identity and Access Management is arguably the single most important area to test. IAM governs who can act, what they can do, and which resources they can access. Common failures include overly permissive policies, long-lived access keys that are not rotated, lack of multi-factor authentication, and roles that grant unnecessary lateral movement across resources. A concrete example: an IAM role with broad permissions can let an attacker list storage buckets, download data, or create new compute instances. During an assessment you should review role policies for wildcards, check whether console access requires MFA, and identify orphaned or unused credentials. A frequent misconception is that complex policy language implies safety; in fact, complexity often hides broad allowances. When you find a policy allowing wide actions, validate the impact by mapping what an attacker could do with those actions. Closing question: if an account with console access lacks MFA and an access key is exposed, how would you prioritize that finding compared to a single misconfigured bucket? Use the Shared Responsibility Model and potential impact to prioritize remediation. Identity and Access Management (IAM) Risks means prioritize reviewing policies, mfa, and key rotation; overly broad policies enable rapid escalation and lateral movement.. In practical terms, why iam is the most critical attack surface in cloud environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › IAM Risks
Definition

Identity and Access Management

IAM controls who can act and what they can do. Look for overly permissive roles, missing MFA, and long-lived credentials.

Checks to run
  • Find wildcard actions or principals in policies
  • Confirm MFA is enforced for console access
  • Locate unused or unrotated access keys
Example
Overly permissive role
A role allowing full storage and compute actions could let an attacker enumerate buckets, download data, and create new instances to persist access. Treat such policies as high priority.
Common misconception
Complex policies are not automatically safe. Complexity can mask broad privileges that enable escalation.
Key Takeaway

Treat IAM findings as high impact: they often enable lateral movement and access to sensitive resources.

screens.title: Open Storage Buckets: A Common Misconfiguration
screens.narratorSegment: Open storage buckets are one of the largest recurring cloud risks. A bucket configured for public read access can leak backups, configuration files, or credentials. Ethical hackers commonly discover these by enumerating known bucket naming patterns or using publicly allowed listing features — but it’s essential to observe without downloading or modifying contents unless authorized. A typical detection method is checking the access control list and bucket policy. For AWS S3 the commands to inspect these settings are available to authorized users via the CLI and were included in the source material; they reveal whether a bucket is public. A realistic example: a bucket with a name indicating production backups that returns a public listing could reveal PII or A P I keys. A common assessor mistake is to assume an 'access denied' response means a bucket doesn't exist; often it means the bucket exists but is not public, which is safer. If you confirm a public bucket, document the contents at a high level and recommend changing the access policy to private or restricting access to authorized roles. Always include: scope confirmation, minimal interaction, and responsible disclosure.

keyIdea.title: Observe, don't interact
keyIdea.text: When finding public buckets, avoid downloading or changing files; document exposure and recommend restricting access or making policies private.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Open Storage Buckets
Problem

Public buckets expose sensitive data

Buckets with public read or list permissions can leak backups, configs, and keys. Discovery is straightforward; responsible handling is not optional.

Detection checklist
  • Check bucket ACL and policy for public principals.
  • Look for IsPublic: true indicators in policy status.
  • Record types of files visible without downloading content.
Command example
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket my-sensitive-data-bucket
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket my-sensitive-data-bucket
If ACL shows READ for AllUsers or policy status IsPublic true, treat as critical and report with remediation.
Assessor caution
Do not download or alter data. Observing directory listings is sufficient for proof of exposure; follow disclosure policies and preserve evidence.
Key Takeaway

Public buckets are discoverable and serious. Document exposure without interacting and recommend restricting access to authorized identities.

screens.title: Network Security Groups and Firewall Rules
screens.narratorSegment: Network security groups and cloud firewall rules control inbound and outbound traffic to cloud resources. A common misconfiguration is allowing unrestricted inbound access to sensitive ports such as SSH, RDP or database ports. For example, a security group that permits SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 allows any internet host to attempt connections, raising the probability of credential abuse or exploitation of unpatched services. During assessments you should enumerate network rules tied to compute instances and check whether ports required for administration are overly open. A useful approach is to classify rules by necessity and exposure: is SSH required from the internet, or only from a VPN or bastion host? Additionally, check whether database instances are attached to public subnets. A common misconception is to assume cloud provider defaults are secure; default templates often permit broader access for convenience. When you find risky rules, recommend narrowing source ranges, introducing bastion hosts, or applying host-level firewalling and MFA-protected access. Closing task: map every inbound rule to an operational justification before labeling it as a vulnerability. Network Security Groups and Firewall Rules means treat wide inbound rules as high-risk; determine necessity and recommend narrowing source ranges or using bastions and private subnets.. In practical terms, how overly-broad inbound rules create cloud-exposed attack surfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Network Security Groups
Definition

Security groups and firewalls

These rules control traffic to cloud resources. Unrestricted inbound rules are a frequent and high-risk misconfiguration.

Checklist
  • Find rules with source 0.0.0.0/0 or equivalent
  • Confirm whether remote admin ports should be public
  • Check if DB instances are publicly reachable
Example
SSH opened to the internet
If SSH is open broadly, attackers can attempt credential-based logins or exploit unpatched services. Recommended remediations include limiting source IPs, requiring a bastion host, and enabling host-level MFA or two-step authentication.
Misconception
Assuming internet-facing services are harmless if they use credentials. Internet exposure multiplies attack surface and should be minimized.
Key Takeaway

Audit all inbound rules; require operational justification for public access and prefer private subnets and bastion patterns.

screens.title: Insecure APIs and Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud providers expose APIs and management interfaces for automation and orchestration. Those same interfaces are attractive targets: if A P I keys or tokens are leaked, attackers can create, modify, or delete resources. An ethical hacker should review access controls on management APIs, check for embedded credentials in code or configuration, and test whether A P I endpoints enforce authentication, authorization, and rate limiting. A simple example is a leaked A P I key in a public repository that grants privileges to create compute instances or list storage. Attackers often use automation against APIs to move quickly, so look for keys, secret rotation gaps, and weak token scopes. A common misconception is to assume network-layer protections alone secure APIs; strong authentication and least-privilege tokens are essential. During testing, avoid attempting destructive A P I calls. Instead, demonstrate control by safely enumerating accessible resources or by requesting read-only data with consent. Your report should describe the token’s effective permissions and recommend immediate rotation and tighter token scopes when you find exposed credentials. Insecure APIs and Interfaces means search for exposed api keys, verify token scopes, and recommend token rotation and least-privilege policies when exposure is found.. In practical terms, how compromised or poorly secured apis enable resource control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Insecure APIs
Process

Assessing API risk

  1. Search for embedded keys or tokens in repos and configs.
  2. Check token scope and rotation policy.
  3. Attempt safe enumeration to validate permissions.
Example
Leaked key in code
If a key in a public repo permits listing buckets, an attacker can discover sensitive storage. Recommend rotating keys immediately and restricting token scopes to minimum privileges.
Misconception
Assuming network protections alone secure APIs. API authentication and least-privilege tokens are core defenses and should be audited.
Key Takeaway

Treat API credentials as highly sensitive; locate, describe the impact, and advise rotation and scope reduction when found.

screens.title: Vulnerable Applications in the Cloud
screens.narratorSegment: Applications deployed in cloud environments carry the same classes of vulnerabilities as on-premise software. S Q L injection, cross-site scripting, insecure deserialization, and other issues can be exploited to access data or run commands that affect cloud resources. For instance, exploiting an S Q L injection might expose database credentials stored in configuration, which an attacker can then use to pivot to backup storage or other services. During cloud assessments, treat application vulnerabilities as potential escalation paths into cloud infrastructure and storage. A common mistake is treating application testing and cloud configuration testing as separate tasks. They are closely related: application flaws can expose secrets or tokens that provide cloud-level access. Practical step: when you find an application vulnerability, map any credentials, keys, or endpoints it reveals, and determine whether those secrets allow access to cloud resources. Misconception: assuming that because the app runs on managed services the cloud provider will prevent exploitation. Providers secure infrastructure but not application logic or plaintext secrets stored by the customer. Key takeaway: include application testing in cloud assessments and follow safe testing rules.

narration.text: Applications deployed in cloud environments carry the same classes of vulnerabilities as on-premise software. S Q L injection, cross-site scripting, insecure deserialization, and other issues can be exploited to access data or run commands that affect cloud resources. For instance, exploiting an S Q L injection might expose database credentials stored in configuration, which an attacker can then use to pivot to backup storage or other services. During cloud assessments, treat application vulnerabilities as potential escalation paths into cloud infrastructure and storage. A common mistake is treating application testing and cloud configuration testing as separate tasks. They are closely related: application flaws can expose secrets or tokens that provide cloud-level access. Practical step: when you find an application vulnerability, map any credentials, keys, or endpoints it reveals, and determine whether those secrets allow access to cloud resources. Misconception: assuming that because the app runs on managed services the cloud provider will prevent exploitation. Providers secure infrastructure but not application logic or plaintext secrets stored by the customer. Key takeaway: include application testing in cloud assessments and follow safe testing rules.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Vulnerable Applications
Definition

Application vulnerabilities as escalation paths

Standard web flaws can reveal credentials, tokens, or configuration that let attackers access cloud resources beyond the application layer.

Assessment focus
  • Map secrets found in app configuration to cloud resources
  • Check for exposed environment variables and config files
  • Assess whether exploitation yields cloud-level control
Example
SQL injection reveals database credentials
If a flaw returns config files containing connection strings, those credentials may grant access to cloud-hosted databases or backups. Follow up by identifying the resource and its access controls.
Misconception
Believing managed services shield application-level issues. They do not; you must test application logic and secret handling.
Key Takeaway

Include application testing in cloud assessments and map any found secrets to the cloud resources they unlock.

screens.title: Insufficient Logging and Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Logging and monitoring are the last line of defense for detecting and containing attacks. In cloud environments, services like activity logs and audit trails record changes and access to resources. If logging is not enabled or logs are not retained and reviewed, attackers can operate for long periods without detection. For an assessment, verify that activity logs are enabled and that critical events—such as IAM changes, object access, and network rule modifications—are recorded. For example, AWS CloudTrail or Azure Activity Log can show who created an access key or made a security group change. A typical assessment step is to trigger a benign read operation under authorization and confirm it is captured in logs, or to review retention and alerting configurations. A common misconception is to assume logs are enabled by default; many accounts require explicit configuration. When you find insufficient logging, recommend enabling audit logs, centralizing logs, and applying alerting for critical events. Final reflective question: how would you demonstrate an attack path without causing changes yet still show that logs are insufficient for detection? Insufficient Logging and Monitoring means verify audit trails are enabled and retained; recommend centralized logs and alerts for critical security events.. In practical terms, why logs matter and how missing telemetry hides attacker activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Logging & Monitoring
Definition

Audit logs and detection

Logs record who did what and when. Without them, attackers can act unnoticed and incidents become harder to investigate.

Checks
  • Confirm activity logs like CloudTrail or Activity Log are enabled
  • Verify retention and centralization policies
  • Check alerting on critical events
Example
Missing logs hide privilege escalation
If IAM changes are not logged or retained, an attacker can escalate privileges and erase traces. Recommend enabling audit logs and alerts for IAM policy changes and key creations.
Misconception
Assuming short log retention is sufficient. Retain logs long enough for investigation and correlate events centrally.
Key Takeaway

Verify logs are enabled, retained, and monitored. Recommend centralization and alerts for security-critical events.

screens.title: Safe Misconfiguration Exploration — Public Bucket Search
screens.narratorSegment: This short, safe activity shows how to discover misconfigured public buckets without interacting with private data. The goal is to observe existence and exposure, not to download or modify files. The recommended approach is to use public search patterns to find likely bucket names and then check only bucket ACL or policy status when you have permission. If you do not have permission, use search engines to observe public listing pages and note filenames without downloading content. A critical precaution: document what you see, avoid data access, and do not attempt destructive or intrusive actions. In a real engagement, always confirm scope and use temporary, least-privilege credentials. After discovery, notify the owner through responsible disclosure and recommend setting the bucket to private or restricting access to required roles. Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Safe Misconfiguration Exploration
Activity

Search for public buckets safely

Use public search patterns and authorized CLI checks to confirm exposure without downloading or changing data.

Example commands (illustrative)
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket my-sensitive-data-bucket
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket my-sensitive-data-bucket
If policy status shows IsPublic true, document the finding and follow disclosure practices. Do not download files.
Safety checklist
  • Confirm scope and authorization before testing.
  • Use temporary least-privilege credentials.
  • Do not download, change, or delete any data you encounter.
  • Document evidence and recommend immediate policy changes.
Pro tip

When in doubt, stop and re-confirm scope. Responsible disclosure builds trust and avoids legal exposure.

screens.title: Assessment Priorities and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When you begin a cloud assessment, prioritize customer-controlled controls and high-impact misconfigurations. Start with identity and access management, then review storage accessibility, network rules, APIs, and application secrets. Use a mapping exercise to tag each resource with its service model and the owner of each control. A frequent mistake is spending time on provider-level infrastructure, which is outside scope and unlikely to reveal customer defects. Another error is assuming the presence of a control implies it’s effective; for instance, logging might be configured but not retained or monitored. Also avoid destructive checks: do not attempt write or delete operations unless expressly authorized. When ranking findings, use impact and ease-of-exploit: an exposed production backup containing PII is both high impact and easy to exploit, while a minor missing header on a test endpoint is low priority. In your report include clear remediation: tighten policies, restrict network ranges, rotate keys, and enable alerting. Final reflective prompt: how would you combine the Shared Responsibility mapping and impact scoring to produce a prioritized remediation plan? Assessment Priorities and Common Mistakes means map ownership, prioritize iam and public data exposures, avoid destructive actions, and recommend concrete remediation in your findings.. Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Assessment Priorities
Process

Prioritize and avoid harm

  1. Map who controls each security layer.
  2. Inspect IAM and public data exposures first.
  3. Confirm logging and retention for detection.
  4. Report with prioritized remediation and evidence.

  • Testing provider-managed infrastructure in-scope

Use ownership mapping and impact scoring to prioritize findings. Always verify scope and avoid actions that could disrupt services or expose you legally.

fullNarratorScript:
Cloud computing changes how systems are built and tested. In this chapter you will learn the three primary service models — infrastructure, platform and software — and why each shifts security tasks between the provider and the customer. We’ll make the Shared Responsibility Model concrete so you know what to test and what the provider already maintains. You will also learn common cloud attack vectors that appear in real engagements: insecure identity and access management, misconfigured storage and network rules, exposed APIs, vulnerable applications, and gaps in logging. Each topic includes practical examples and a safety-first checklist for hands-on assessments. For example, an open storage bucket can expose backups or secrets; understanding which party controls that configuration is essential before reporting a finding. Throughout the lesson I’ll describe realistic attacker paths and common assessor mistakes, and I’ll close with a short simulated activity you can run safely in public data. By the end, you’ll recognize what to test, how to prioritize findings, and how to avoid causing harm during an assessment.

These learning objectives give you a clear map of what competence looks like for cloud security assessment. First, you will learn to differentiate cloud service models and deployment options so you can determine who owns each security control. A concrete example is recognizing that in IaaS you must patch the operating system, while a SaaS application’s runtime is managed by the provider. Second, you will explain the Shared Responsibility Model and apply it during testing. That means you will identify provider-controlled components versus customer-managed components before designing an engagement. Third, you will identify typical cloud attack vectors like insecure IAM, open storage buckets, and exposed APIs, and practice how to detect them. Finally, you will analyze misconfigurations and interpret logging gaps so you can score findings accurately and recommend actionable remediation. Each objective ties to a practical task: classify a resource, examine an IAM policy, check a storage ACL, and review cloud logs for suspicious activity.

These practical objectives translate knowledge into testable skills. You will practice inspecting IAM policies to spot overly permissive roles and unrotated keys, and you will test for multi-factor authentication gaps. You will perform safe discovery for misconfigured storage — observing publicly exposed buckets without downloading or modifying data. You will audit network security rules to find unintended inbound access, such as wide-open SSH or database ports. You will also learn to evaluate logging coverage so you can judge whether an attacker could remain undetected. Each objective includes a verification step: read a policy, confirm MFA, query a bucket’s public ACL, and check whether activity logging is enabled. That verification step is what counts toward competency. Remember: do not make changes to a customer environment without explicit authorization; instead, reproduce findings with permissive test accounts or in a controlled lab.

Start by making the service models concrete. Infrastructure as a Service gives you virtual machines and networking; you are responsible for the operating system, applications, and data on those machines. Platform as a Service provides a managed runtime and platform components — you typically deploy code but do not manage the underlying OS. Software as a Service delivers a complete application where the provider manages almost everything, but you must still control user identities and data within the app. A practical example: if a company runs a web server on an IaaS virtual machine, it must apply OS patches and configure firewalls. If the same company deploys the web app to a PaaS offering, the provider manages the runtime patching, but the app code and configuration remain the customer's responsibility. A common misconception is to assume SaaS needs no security testing; in reality, misconfigured user roles, weak authentication, or exposed integrations in SaaS can still lead to breaches. Key takeaway: determine which model a target resource implements before you design tests. That classification directly informs which controls you inspect and which findings you report.

The Shared Responsibility Model is the foundation for cloud security testing. In simple terms, the cloud provider secures the underlying infrastructure — the physical data centers, hardware, and core virtualization — while the customer secures resources they deploy inside that infrastructure, such as data, applications, operating systems, and network configuration. For example, a provider ensures the hypervisor is patched and that physical access controls exist, but it is the customer’s duty to rotate their access keys, configure secure network rules, and harden application code. For an ethical hacker this distinction matters because misconfigurations and application vulnerabilities in the customer’s responsibility area are where you will find the majority of exploitable issues. A common misconception is to test provider infrastructure in a live engagement; doing so can violate terms and cause harm. Instead, identify which controls the customer manages and prioritize those for inspection. Practical step: create a simple mapping for each resource you encounter that labels which side manages the OS, network policies, data encryption, identity, and logging. That map becomes your test scope and helps avoid false positives or misattributed findings.

Identity and Access Management is arguably the single most important area to test. IAM governs who can act, what they can do, and which resources they can access. Common failures include overly permissive policies, long-lived access keys that are not rotated, lack of multi-factor authentication, and roles that grant unnecessary lateral movement across resources. A concrete example: an IAM role with broad permissions can let an attacker list storage buckets, download data, or create new compute instances. During an assessment you should review role policies for wildcards, check whether console access requires MFA, and identify orphaned or unused credentials. A frequent misconception is that complex policy language implies safety; in fact, complexity often hides broad allowances. When you find a policy allowing wide actions, validate the impact by mapping what an attacker could do with those actions. Closing question: if an account with console access lacks MFA and an access key is exposed, how would you prioritize that finding compared to a single misconfigured bucket? Use the Shared Responsibility Model and potential impact to prioritize remediation. Identity and Access Management (IAM) Risks means prioritize reviewing policies, mfa, and key rotation; overly broad policies enable rapid escalation and lateral movement.. In practical terms, why iam is the most critical attack surface in cloud environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Open storage buckets are one of the largest recurring cloud risks. A bucket configured for public read access can leak backups, configuration files, or credentials. Ethical hackers commonly discover these by enumerating known bucket naming patterns or using publicly allowed listing features — but it’s essential to observe without downloading or modifying contents unless authorized. A typical detection method is checking the access control list and bucket policy. For AWS S3 the commands to inspect these settings are available to authorized users via the CLI and were included in the source material; they reveal whether a bucket is public. A realistic example: a bucket with a name indicating production backups that returns a public listing could reveal PII or A P I keys. A common assessor mistake is to assume an 'access denied' response means a bucket doesn't exist; often it means the bucket exists but is not public, which is safer. If you confirm a public bucket, document the contents at a high level and recommend changing the access policy to private or restricting access to authorized roles. Always include: scope confirmation, minimal interaction, and responsible disclosure.

Network security groups and cloud firewall rules control inbound and outbound traffic to cloud resources. A common misconfiguration is allowing unrestricted inbound access to sensitive ports such as SSH, RDP or database ports. For example, a security group that permits SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 allows any internet host to attempt connections, raising the probability of credential abuse or exploitation of unpatched services. During assessments you should enumerate network rules tied to compute instances and check whether ports required for administration are overly open. A useful approach is to classify rules by necessity and exposure: is SSH required from the internet, or only from a VPN or bastion host? Additionally, check whether database instances are attached to public subnets. A common misconception is to assume cloud provider defaults are secure; default templates often permit broader access for convenience. When you find risky rules, recommend narrowing source ranges, introducing bastion hosts, or applying host-level firewalling and MFA-protected access. Closing task: map every inbound rule to an operational justification before labeling it as a vulnerability. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Those same interfaces are attractive targets: if A P I keys or tokens are leaked, attackers can create, modify, or delete resources. A simple example is a leaked A P I key in a public repository that grants privileges to create compute instances or list storage. During testing, avoid attempting destructive A P I calls. Instead, demonstrate control by safely enumerating accessible resources or by requesting read-only data with consent. Your report should describe the token’s effective permissions and recommend immediate rotation and tighter token scopes when you find exposed credentials. When you begin a cloud assessment, prioritize customer-controlled controls and high-impact misconfigurations. Start with identity and access management, then review storage accessibility, network rules, APIs, and application secrets. Use a mapping exercise to tag each resource with its service model and the owner of each control. A frequent mistake is spending time on provider-level infrastructure, which is outside scope and unlikely to reveal customer defects. Another error is assuming the presence of a control implies it’s effective; for instance, logging might be configured but not retained or monitored. Also avoid destructive checks: do not attempt write or delete operations unless expressly authorized. When ranking findings, use impact and ease-of-exploit: an exposed production backup containing PII is both high impact and easy to exploit, while a minor missing header on a test endpoint is low priority. In your report include clear remediation: tighten policies, restrict network ranges, rotate keys, and enable alerting. Here are compact reminders of the core concepts from this chapter. First, IaaS provides virtual infrastructure where customers manage the OS and applications, PaaS provides a managed platform for deploying code, and SaaS delivers an application managed by the provider. These distinctions determine what you test and who is responsible for remediation. Second, the Shared Responsibility Model separates 'security of the cloud' from 'security in the cloud' — providers handle infrastructure while customers secure their deployments, data, and identity. Third, Identity and Access Management is a primary attack surface: check policies, MFA settings, and key rotation. Keep these three concepts in mind as you design assessments and prioritize findings. Here are the remaining core concepts to remember. Misconfiguration — including open storage buckets and permissive network rules — is a primary cause of cloud breaches. Insecure APIs and exposed keys enable attackers to control resources, so always search for embedded credentials and rotate compromised tokens. Finally, operational practices matter: insufficient logging and monitoring allow attackers to remain undetected. As you conduct assessments, pair technical findings with safe, non-destructive verification steps and clear remediation: restrict access, rotate credentials, enable logging, and centralize alerts. These practical rules help you deliver findings that secure cloud workloads while avoiding service disruption or legal risk.
